lines.text: Alpine salt mines, an empire that ruled half of Europe, and a capital of music. This is the story of Austria, from the Iceman to the European Union.
More than five thousand years ago, a man died high in the Alps. Frozen in the ice, he was found in 1991, and named Otzi.
Later, salt miners at Hallstatt grew rich, and gave their village's name to a whole early Iron Age culture of Europe.
By around the year 100 the Romans held the Danube, with a camp called Vindobona. It would grow into Vienna.
In the west, Salzburg grew around its church, a city that prince-archbishops would rule for centuries.
In 976 a margrave was given a march on the Danube. From that border land grew Austria.
Then came the Habsburgs, a family from Switzerland who would rule Austria, Spain and the Holy Roman Empire for centuries.
In Vienna, work began on St Stephen's Cathedral, whose Gothic spire became the symbol of the city.
In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged Vienna. A relief force led by the Polish king Jan Sobieski broke the siege, and the Ottomans began to retreat.
Soon after, the Habsburgs began their summer palace of Schonbrunn on the edge of Vienna.
From 1740 Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg lands, fighting for her throne and reforming schools, taxes and the army. She had sixteen children.
Joseph Haydn wrote more than a hundred symphonies and helped shape the string quartet, the start of Vienna's golden age of music.
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, played in public as a small child, and wrote more than six hundred works before dying in Vienna at thirty-five.
Beethoven came to Vienna from Germany to study with Haydn. Even as he went deaf, he kept composing, and the Romantic age began.
Klemens von Metternich, Austria's great statesman, would lead Europe's rebuilding after Napoleon and guard the old order for decades.
Franz Schubert wrote some six hundred songs in a short life. He died at thirty-one, and much of his music was heard only after his death.
In 1804, as the Holy Roman Empire failed, Francis the second proclaimed an Austrian Empire, ruling from Bohemia to northern Italy.
After Napoleon's fall, Europe's powers met in Vienna to redraw the map. Their balance kept a general war away for a long time.
Johann Strauss the younger, the waltz king, would set Vienna dancing to The Blue Danube.
In 1842 the Vienna Philharmonic gave its first concerts. Its New Year's Concert is now heard around the world.
In Vienna, Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, the talking cure, and his ideas about the unconscious spread far beyond medicine.
Gustav Klimt led the Vienna Secession, and painted The Kiss in shimmering gold.
In 1867 the empire became the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, one emperor ruling many peoples across Central Europe.
On the twenty-eighth of June 1914, the heir Franz Ferdinand was shot in Sarajevo. Within weeks Europe was at war, and the empire would not survive it.
What was left became a small republic. In March 1938 Hitler's Germany annexed it, and Austria disappeared from the map.
Niki Lauda, born in Vienna in 1949, would win three Formula One titles and return to racing after a terrible crash.
After the war Austria was occupied by the Allies, until the treaty of 1955 made it free again, and neutral.
A decade later, The Sound of Music brought Salzburg and its mountains to cinemas all over the world.
And in 1995 Austria joined the European Union, alongside Finland and Sweden.
From the Iceman to Europe's heart, Austria's mountains have seen empires rise, fall and make music.
